questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that an incident response lifecycle needs to be defined in advance, rather than figured out during an actual incident?
options: Because Salesforce requires a written IR plan to be submitted before Shield can be purchased
Because an incident is exactly the wrong moment to invent a process -- people are stressed, information is incomplete, and early decisions often matter more than later ones
Because incident response only applies to orgs with Transaction Security Policies enabled
Because IR plans are only useful after an incident has already been fully resolved
questions.explain: The value of defining the lifecycle in advance is precisely that an incident is a high-stress, information-poor moment -- having the process already decided means less is being improvised when it matters most.

questions.q: What is the key difference between the "containment" and "eradication" phases of incident response?
options: They are the same step, just described with two different words
Eradication always happens before containment in a correctly run incident
Containment limits ongoing damage immediately, often with a temporary measure, before root cause is fully understood; eradication removes the actual underlying cause once it is understood
Containment only applies to Apex code issues; eradication only applies to configuration issues
questions.explain: Containment is an immediate, sometimes temporary damage-limiting action (freezing an account, revoking a session); eradication is the deeper fix addressing the actual root cause -- skipping eradication risks the incident recurring once containment is lifted.

questions.q: In the lifecycle-to-tool mapping, which Salesforce-specific capability would most directly support the "containment" phase for a compromised user account?
options: Running a Health Check scan
Rotating the Shield Platform Encryption tenant secret
Writing a new data flow diagram
A Transaction Security Policy action such as freezing the user or ending the session
questions.explain: Transaction Security Policy actions like freeze user or end session are immediate, real-time containment measures -- they limit ongoing damage right now, distinct from Health Check (a governance score) or tenant secret rotation (a deeper eradication-phase action).

questions.q: Per this lesson, what does an accurate, current data flow diagram (from Lesson 13) provide during the "detection and analysis" phase?
options: A starting map of exactly where sensitive data could have gone, instead of discovering the integration landscape for the first time mid-incident
It automatically contains the incident without any human action
It replaces the need for Event Log Files during an investigation
It is only useful during the lessons-learned phase, not detection and analysis
questions.explain: A current data flow diagram lets investigators start detection and analysis already knowing the data's possible paths and boundaries, rather than having to reconstruct the integration landscape from scratch while the incident is still unfolding.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the "lessons learned" phase, per this lesson?
options: To assign blame to the individual responsible for the incident
A deliberate after-action review that feeds findings back into the architecture review process, so the same gap doesn't recur
To immediately delete all logs related to the incident
To skip containment and eradication if the incident turns out to be minor
questions.explain: Lessons learned is explicitly about feeding the incident's specific finding back into Lesson 11's review checklist, so future reviews specifically check for that gap -- a forward-looking governance step, not a blame exercise.
